clue.text: Entertainment for the sweet-toothed?

parts.note: read as a work to entertain readers, it is Graham Greene's 1938 novel; read literally, it is the hard pink stick of seaside candy sold at a Sussex resort

explanation.surface: A question about what treat would amuse someone who loves sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: The seaside rock is a stick of hard candy sold at British resorts, its name running through it in letters; the novel takes its title from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's novel is a literary entertainment, and the candy of that name is a confection for those fond of sugar.

clue.text: "Nature's gives nothing, but doth lend" (Shakespeare)

parts.note: a quotation with a word missing: the solver supplies the noun from Sonnet 4 that follows Nature's, meaning what Nature hands down

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare quoted with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Shakespeare's Sonnet 4, which tells a young man that his beauty is only on loan from Nature.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a legacy or gift left to someone, which the sonnet says Nature only lends.

clue.text: Tarkington finally offered Josephine's

parts.note: Booth Tarkington's last novel, published in 1945, was titled after a likeness of a woman called Josephine

explanation.surface: A remark that an American novelist at last gave something belonging to Josephine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' is not a last-letter signal: it refers to Booth Tarkington's final novel, Image of Josephine (1945).
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Tarkington's last book names a likeness or representation of Josephine.

clue.text: Shakespearean suitor morphs into horse

indicators.note: morphs means changes shape, so the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare character transforms into a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'morphs' rearranges the nine letters of INTO HORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Taming of the Shrew this man woos Bianca, Katherina's younger sister, disguised as a music teacher.

clue.text: Lubricates art

definitions.meaning: greases or applies a slippery fluid to machinery
paintings done in pigment mixed with linseed and similar media

explanation.definitionFit: To grease a machine is to apply lubricant, and paintings in that medium are known by the same plural word.

clue.text: "Walter ordered a broiled fish and a bottle of" (Patricia Highsmith, The Blunderer)

definitions.text: "Walter ordered a broiled fish and a bottle of" (Patricia Highsmith, The Blunderer)

parts.words: "Walter ordered a broiled fish and a bottle of" (Patricia Highsmith, The Blunderer)
parts.note: a quotation whose last word is left for the solver: the white wine Walter orders with his fish in Highsmith's novel

explanation.surface: A line from a Patricia Highsmith thriller about a man ordering dinner, cut off before the wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver completes the sentence from The Blunderer (1954); a white wine with fish is the natural choice.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names a white wine grape from Germany's Rhine and Mosel, often drunk with fish.

clue.text: Firbank's whim places church on this island

indicators.note: the island with the church placed after it on the page makes the whim, so taking that abbreviation away from the whim leaves the island

parts.note: Ronald Firbank's 1917 novel is Caprice, and a caprice is a whim
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Ronald Firbank, on a whim, builds a church on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: put CE (church) on the end of the island and you get CAPRICE, a Firbank novel title meaning whim.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian island in the Bay of Naples, famous for the Blue Grotto.

clue.text: Bold harp composition from Windsor tapster

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters of the two words are arranged anew

explanation.surface: A bold harp piece from someone at Windsor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges BOLD HARP; 'from' is a link. In The Merry Wives of Windsor Falstaff's follower becomes a tapster at the Garter Inn.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff's red-nosed crony takes a job drawing ale at the Garter Inn in The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: Composer in firm following directions

indicators.note: following means the firm's letters come after the compass points

parts.note: E, N, E and S are compass directions: east, north, east, south
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A composer works in a company, taking instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'directions' supplies four compass points here, ENES, a liberty the setter takes; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: George Enescu, the Romanian composer of the Romanian Rhapsodies, was known in France by this spelling.

clue.text: Dance play

definitions.meaning: a square dance for four couples, popular in the nineteenth century
Noel Coward's 1952 comedy of that title

explanation.definitionFit: It is both a square dance for four couples and the title of a Noel Coward stage comedy.

clue.text: Simple as the pleasures of Bowles ()

definitions.meaning: Jane Bowles's 1966 story collection is ... Pleasures

explanation.definitionFit: Something unadorned is simple, and Jane Bowles titled her story collection after unfussy pleasures.

clue.text: Henry's uncle of Hardy's Exonbury

definitions.meaning: in Shakespeare's Henry V the king's uncle is the Duke of this title
Thomas Hardy's Wessex novels disguise the Devon cathedral city as Exonbury

explanation.definitionFit: The duke who is Henry V's uncle takes his title from the Devon city that Hardy's Wessex calls Exonbury.

clue.text: Atlas issue

parts.note: not a volume of maps but the offspring of the Titan who holds up the sky: his seven daughters, who became a star cluster

explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the seven sisters of the star cluster were daughters of the Titan who bore the heavens.

clue.text: Bennett's girl of the Roman road

definitions.text: Bennett's girl of the Roman road

parts.words: Bennett's girl of the Roman road
parts.note: Arnold Bennett's 1904 novel is about a girl of Watling Street, the Roman road from Kent to Wales

explanation.surface: A young woman from an ancient highway in Bennett's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Watling Street is a Roman road across England; Arnold Bennett's novel Teresa of Watling Street (1904) names its heroine after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett's heroine is named in the title of his novel set on Watling Street, a Roman road.

clue.text: Storytelling uncle perhaps

definitions.meaning: the act of recounting or narrating a tale
an uncle is one example of a family member

explanation.definitionFit: Narrating a tale is one sense, and a kinsman such as an uncle is another.

clue.text: With which to make an incisive design statement

definitions.text: With which to make an incisive design statement

parts.words: With which to make an incisive design statement
parts.note: incisive is meant literally: the design is cut into the surface of a gem or plate, the reverse of a cameo

explanation.surface: An instrument for making a sharp, bold remark about design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incisive' looks like 'sharp-witted' but means cut in: an engraved design sunk below the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a design engraved or incised into hard material, used for seals and printing plates.

clue.text: Subject matter for Allen and Besant

definitions.text: Subject matter for Allen and Besant

parts.words: Subject matter for Allen and Besant
parts.note: the material that gave titles to books by these Victorian writers

explanation.surface: A question of what topic two Victorian writers shared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject matter' is literal: the material named in their titles, such as Besant's The Alabaster Box.
explanation.definitionFit: The white translucent stone named in titles by these writers is the matter they wrote about.

clue.text: His autobiography reveals a perfect stranger

definitions.text: His autobiography reveals a perfect stranger

parts.words: His autobiography reveals a perfect stranger
parts.note: the poet P. J. ... titled his 1966 memoir The Perfect Stranger

explanation.surface: A man's memoir shows him to be someone nobody knew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a perfect stranger' is the title of P. J. Kavanagh's memoir, The Perfect Stranger (1966), not a description of him.
explanation.definitionFit: The English poet P. J. Kavanagh wrote a memoir called The Perfect Stranger.

clue.text: Let in some sort of light for Woolf character

indicators.note: in means the word for let is placed inside the word for a kind of light

parts.note: daylight is one sort of light, giving day
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: Letting some light in for a character of Virginia Woolf's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some sort of light' is daylight shortened to its first word; 'in' is the container signal, so the verb for let sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa, the society hostess of Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel, gives the book its title.

clue.text: On several occasions he wrote poems

definitions.text: On several occasions he wrote poems

parts.words: On several occasions he wrote poems
parts.note: points to Austin ..., Victorian writer of light occasional verse in old French forms

explanation.surface: A poet who wrote verses now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On several occasions' means occasional verse, poems written for particular occasions, Austin Dobson's speciality.
explanation.definitionFit: Austin Dobson was a Victorian poet known for occasional verse and vers de société.

clue.text: Quiet musketeer engages sympathy

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
Athos is one of Dumas's three musketeers

explanation.surface: A silent musketeer draws compassion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engages' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality in writing that stirs pity and sorrow in the reader.

clue.text: Second journalist on the French Connection

parts.note: a hack is a journalist
le is the French for the

explanation.surface: A second reporter is working on the French Connection.
explanation.walkthrough: The French Connection is a 1971 film, but here 'the French' gives LE and 'Connection' is the definition; 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-shaped metal link used for coupling chains is a connecting piece.

clue.text: Wager your chap heard poet

parts.note: a bet is a wager

indicators.note: heard means the phrase for your chap is spoken aloud

parts.note: your chap is your man, said in Irish fashion as yer man

explanation.surface: A bet on a man rumoured to be a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' turns 'your chap', said 'yer man', into the sound of JEMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: John Betjeman was Britain's Poet Laureate from 1972 to 1984.

clue.text: Macabre artist measures alternative

parts.note: an en is a printer's measure of type width, so ens are measures
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A gruesome painter takes measures as an alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: James Ensor, the Belgian painter, filled his canvases with skeletons and grotesque masks.

clue.text: Spanish novelist gets German agreement to follow wild boar

indicators.note: to follow means the German word comes after the anagram
wild means the letters of boar run loose and are rearranged

parts.note: ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: A Spanish writer agrees in German to chase a wild pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' is the anagram signal on 'boar', and 'to follow' puts the German yes after the shuffled letters; 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pio Baroja was a Basque novelist of Spain's Generation of '98.

clue.text: How Cicero would speak (at zero speed) ()

parts.note: O is the figure zero
rate is speed, as in a rate of knots

explanation.surface: The way a Roman would talk while standing still.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is the wordplay; 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal speech, as the Roman statesman did in the Senate.

clue.text: Many support poet in his work

indicators.note: support means one piece sits beneath the other in this down clue

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe was an American poet
M is a thousand in Roman numerals, a large number

explanation.surface: Lots of people back a poet in his writing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'support' puts M below POE; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of verse is what a poet produces.

clue.text: Former pupils take Old English woodwinds ()

indicators.note: take means the former pupils hold the other piece within them

parts.note: OBs are old boys, former pupils of a school

explanation.surface: Ex-students take up Old English wind instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: Old boys (OBs) is the British term for former pupils of a school; 'take' is the container signal, so the abbreviation for Old English goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-reed instruments of the woodwind section.

clue.text: P. H. Newby found many from whom to enquire

parts.note: a lot means many
someone to enquire from is someone to ask, giving to ask

explanation.surface: A novelist found plenty of people to question.
explanation.walkthrough: P. H. Newby's 1973 novel A Lot to Ask is the definition; 'found' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: P. H. Newby, first winner of the Booker Prize, wrote a 1973 novel of this title.

clue.text: English writer — German rage he stirs up

indicators.note: stirs up means the letters are mixed together into a new order

explanation.surface: An English writer gets a German angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirs up' rearranges GERMAN RAGE HE.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist of The Power and the Glory and The Third Man.
